t: Why Rote Learning Is What Kept Me in Teaching
q: But there’s a difference between watching students successfully complete a task in a lesson and having them actually retain or learn something. Earlier in my career, I wasn’t always particularly good at distinguishing between the two.
If the accusation is that ‘rote learning’ involves students remembering what we’ve taught them, then frankly, I don’t know why that ever became something we were supposed to apologise for doing.

I was viewing somewhere between 30 to 100+ mini whiteboards of student attempts at questions every single lesson. Every time I taught a new skill, I could see almost immediately where students were making errors, what those errors were, and, most importantly, I could immediately adjust my teaching to correct those errors.
I’ve said it before, but there is a real irony in taking the students who need the most support and giving them the least exposure to the content they need.
The instructional harm of too much guidance for a student who doesn’t need it is far less than the instructional harm of not providing enough guidance to a student who does need it.
My students are busy throughout most of the lesson. I sometimes joke that they don’t have time to bend the rules.
Evidence should inform what we do, but it doesn’t have to dictate who we are while doing it.
I didn’t need more freedom to write lessons or come up with a never-before-seen activity to teach linear equations. I needed the time, knowledge and support to become a better teacher.
The approach so often criticised for turning teachers into mindless robots actually made me feel like I could be more myself in the classroom.

t: Why Habits of Gratitude Are the Mark of a Thriving Christian School
q: Gratitude isn’t urgent, and it isn’t efficient. It takes time and intention.
Every good thing in our hands was first handed to us. Nancy DeMoss has observed that gratitude is the natural outflow of a humble heart. In other words, gratitude flows downstream of humility.
Campuses run on urgency. I’ve often called principals and deans expert emergency responders, putting out fires all day, every day.

In more than a quarter century of Christian school leadership, I’ve learned many lessons and become convinced of a few things. Here is one of them: when you strategically recognize what you want repeated, it will be repeated.
Most people delete emails of gratitude. Most people keep handwritten thank-you notes.
Schools rarely get to gather their entire community. When you do, use that moment strategically to shape grateful hearts.
Name someone every time you address your team. Whenever I speak to my team in a public setting, I try to thank someone in the room for a specific, recent contribution to our school.
Before your head hits the pillow, or before most of your staff wakes up, send a text or email thanking them for all they did to help your school thrive.
x: Gratitude is not urgent or efficient, which is exactly why a visible habit of it signals intentional, thriving school leadership.
Because gratitude flows downstream of humility, leaders who build thankfulness are also preparing their communities to resolve inevitable conflicts.
Chris Hobbs, a Christian school leader of more than twenty-five years, argues that the habits of gratitude visible on a campus are a reliable barometer of how well the school is thriving.
Recognition is a culture tool: strategically thanking the people who model the qualities you want repeated is one of the surest ways to shape a school.
Handwritten notes outlast emails, and opening a leadership meeting by having each leader write a note to a staff member turns appreciation into a routine.

t: Understanding Their Feelings Isn't Enough
q: I have heard parents say “I feel your feelings.” I understand the sentiment and I know it is often said with love, but acknowledging the feelings is only the first part.
We need to give them opportunities to pause, reflect on their thoughts, consider different options and decide the best way to respond.
Knowing they are understood is powerful, but helping them realise what to do next is the key to unlocking their potential. This is a skill, and one that we can nurture and build together.
A 2020 meta-analysis explored whether self-regulation in childhood relates to higher achievement, interpersonal behaviours and mental and physical health.
It found evidence that regulation in childhood is linked to better outcomes in all of those. So we can conclude, from the study, that self-regulation matters.
Knowing the difference between what we feel and what is fact. We may be feeling an emotion (like anger), but anger doesn’t define us.
Being aware of mistakes and taking responsibility. This may be one of the hardest skills to develop. It’s always easier to blame someone else.
And just a reminder that critical thinking is not the opposite of emotions, but a guide that stops emotions from ruling us.

t: The Workplace Broke Gen Z and Then Blamed Them for It
q: The proportion of young workers who feel comfortable discussing stress with their line manager fell from 75% in the 2024 Burnout Report to 56% in 2025. This is a collapse, in a single year, that should alarm anyone who believes manager relationships are the foundation of good mental health at work.
Deloitte’s 2024 Gen Z and Millennial Survey, drawing on responses from over 22,000 people across 44 countries, found that 40% of Gen Z respondents feel stressed most or all of the time.

They came of age watching institutions (governments, banks, employers) fail at scale. They face housing costs that would make their managers’ first purchases unrecognisable. They carry student debt that previous generations did not.

The psychological contract (work hard, demonstrate loyalty, be rewarded with security and progression) has been demonstrably broken enough times that trusting it requires a leap of faith that the evidence does not support.

Framing Gen Z’s workplace behaviour as a generational character deficiency is both inaccurate and commercially costly. The organisations that treat younger workers’ expectations around flexibility, mental health support, and meaningful work as unreasonable demands are systematically losing access to a significant proportion of the available talent pool.

The people most likely to characterise Gen Z as difficult are often those whose own early career was shaped by very different structural conditions: lower housing costs, more stable employment contracts, a clearer relationship between effort and reward, and a labour market not yet reshaped by AI.

Their template for what ‘normal’ working life looks like does not map onto the world their younger colleagues inhabit. That is a failure of contextual analysis; and contextual analysis is supposed to be a core competency of leadership.
As a result, the question we need to ask is ‘What are we asking them to get on with, and does that question survive scrutiny?’ Most of the time, if you ask it honestly, it does not.

t: Stop Waiting for Students to Want to Do the Work
q: That shifting format is extraneous load in its purest form, work the test demands that has nothing to do with the material, and the hagwons exist to carry students through it.
In effect he is asking the parents to take extraneous load off their children and offering the results as proof.

For Lion, with his gifts, the essay formats and test strategies that Fortress teaches are extraneous, effort that does nothing for the learning he wants his students to do, and he can afford to step around them. For students without his gifts those same formats and strategies are the intrinsic material of the task, because the goal they are working towards is a seat at an elite university.
Cognitive load theory was built to describe a lesson. Lee gives these loads fifteen years.
She can tap her intrinsic inquisitive nature about how education actually works because a demand that began outside her plan, her family’s primary needs, gave her years inside the work.
For some students the blank page is extraneous load, and AI clears the blockage. For others the blank page is the intrinsic load, the struggle that builds the schema, and AI removes the struggle.
What if demands that begin as extraneous become the task that lights our intrinsic fires pushing us towards greater agility or deeper expertise?
So my advice is to stop waiting for students to want to do the work. Give them the work and a goal worth having, with enough structure that the pathway forward is clear and acheivable.

q: Instead of asking, “Why didn’t this child or young person take the opportunity?”, perhaps we should ask, “What did the opportunity look like from where they were standing?

Researchers at JRF identify 686 neighbourhoods, home to 5.7 million people, facing what it describes as a “double disadvantage”, high levels of socioeconomic deprivation combined with weaker social infrastructure.
The income may look similar on a spreadsheet but the lived experience can be very different.

Children, young people and families do, of course, make choices. But choices are made and consequences are felt within different contexts and conditions, and place shapes the menu from which choices are understood and made.

The problem is not that disadvantaged children somehow lack dreams, but often they lack visibility and opportunity. It is difficult for a young person to choose something that they do not know exists.
Making opportunity visible is not about raising aspiration as though ambition needs importing into communities from elsewhere – it is about widening the field of vision.
Instead, this work means recognising their potential role as civic anchors; places which can convene, connect, and help strengthen the wider social infrastructure surrounding children and families.
Opportunity is a very tangible experience for a young person. It is the the place where it is signposted, the people that help them understand it, and the transport that gets them there.

t: Organizational Structure for Software-Defined Products
q: A company can somehow get by with a missing strategy and bad product decisions. An unclear organizational structure brings it to a standstill.
The first reaction is almost always: It’s not my part, it’s someone else’s. Before I take responsibility, you’ll have to prove that my parts are the cause of the problem.
Separating the goal from the path is pure mission command in Moltke’s sense. The product owner decides the what and the why. The team decides the how.

The greatest weakness lies in separating responsibility for the work from responsibility for the people. Whoever decides on an employee’s development is not responsible for what that employee delivers.
The greatest weakness is dependence on the boss. The organization is only as good as the people deciding at the center.
Every known organizational form has advantages and disadvantages. My proposal tries to combine the essential advantages and soften the disadvantages as much as possible.
In many companies, an executive’s rank is measured by how many people report to them. The more people, the more important the boss.
Staff positions are often abolished today because they are seen as a privilege. They’re not a privilege. They’re a necessary resource.

t: How to Win People Over
q: Perhaps the better question isn’t how to win a negotiation, but what needs to happen for everyone to feel they’ve got a good deal.
In these situations, there’s a difference between getting someone to do something and getting them genuinely on board.
But what if, instead of focusing on how to get them to do the work, you focused on why they might want to do it?
The point isn’t to tell people what they want to hear. It’s to understand what matters to them well enough to find a solution that works for both of you.
If they felt pressured into accepting a price that wasn’t worthwhile for them, they might be less keen to work with you again or put less effort into the relationship if they do.
If you persuade Amy to take on the extra work by promising her exposure to senior stakeholders, make sure those introductions happen.
We need to be careful not to use that understanding simply to get more out of them.

Winning people over isn’t about finding the perfect argument, pushing harder or having the last word. It’s about understanding the person in front of you, finding a way forward that benefits both of you and leaving them feeling they would happily work with you again.

t: Do, not Be is the operative word
q: Career readiness is starting too soon. Schools (middle school, in my local district, and then again in high school) are forcing kids to think too much, too soon, about being, at the expense of doing.

When we ask children “identity” questions we are inviting a “yes” or a “no” – “no, I’m not like that”, for example. A more effective approach is to offer up opportunities to do, and then let children naturally decide how that doing feels.

Identity takes years to develop and healthy identities are those that emerge from experiences. When young people adopt a label and then act in kind, their identity is foreclosed: brittle, uneasy, and insecure.

Children who were invited to do science in that one-off activity over the course of the year showed greater interest in and greater efficacy of accomplishment, in science-related schoolwork and activities. The effect was powerful!

When we signal identity, we are drawing attention to group-level dimensions, and kids are thinking: “do I fit with that group?” If children don’t see a resemblance, then they feel like they don’t belong, and anxiety or disinterest is activated.
Instead of who do you want to be when you grow up, we should simply say what do you want to do when you grow up? Instead of “let’s be poets” for the writing workshop, we say “let’s write some poems
This kind of change can happen right away! No need to change the curriculum — just change the language and the adjust the activities that already exist.

t: You Can Tell a Lot About a Man by How He Treats Women https://thewaysofagentleman.substack.com/p/you-can-tell-a-lot-about-a-man-by-how-he-treats-women
q: Every woman you meet has a life beyond the few moments you spend with her. She has parents who love her. She has hopes, fears, ambitions, insecurities, and dreams for her future.
One approach treats a woman as a means to satisfy our desires; the other recognizes that how we treat a woman is a reflection of our own character.
If the relationship ends, allow it to end with dignity. Don’t humiliate her afterward by sharing intimate details with your friends.

Pornography encourages a man to separate a woman’s body from her humanity. The person on the screen becomes something to be consumed for gratification, and that mindset probably won’t stay confined to a screen.
Not every desire deserves to be satisfied. There are a lot of things a man might want that wisdom tells him to resist.
Self-control isn’t a weakness; it’s one of the clearest demonstrations of strength. Any man can surrender to his appetites, but it takes discipline to govern them.
It’s easy to behave respectfully when a woman is standing right in front of you. The bigger test comes when she isn’t standing there.

The answer is not simply to work harder, acquire another qualification or learn a few new AI tools. It requires a different approach to understanding the world, making decisions and exercising influence.
The danger is no longer simply not knowing enough. It is not knowing what you need to know.

Waiting for certainty can become as dangerous as acting prematurely. The challenge is to distinguish reliable evidence from plausible speculation, recognise competing explanations and understand the implications of different choices.

AI can contribute enormously to this process. It can challenge assumptions, examine alternatives and expose weaknesses in an argument. But it can also generate convincing errors and misleading confidence.

t: Screen Time and AI Need Different Questions
q: The screen-time conversation asks how much time children spend with media, what they encounter, and what that time replaces. The AI conversation also asks who is doing the thinking, whether information is accurate, whose work is being presented, and what happens to student data.

When we collapse those questions into one argument about devices, we make it harder to address either well. A limit on screen minutes cannot tell us whether a student understands an AI-assisted answer.

A school should be able to explain why a digital activity deserves students’ time. Calling something educational does not automatically make it worthwhile. Nor does an engaging app earn unlimited access to the school day.

Consider a teacher using AI to generate possible discussion questions, then checking and adapting them before a device-free seminar. The teacher has used AI. Students have not added a minute of screen exposure.

A 2025 high-school mathematics experiment makes the distinction concrete. Students using an open-ended AI tool performed better during assisted practice but worse on a later unassisted assessment than students without it.
Better-looking work and stronger understanding are different outcomes. We need to check both.

t: Oracy In Practice
q: I think there are quite a few false binaries going on which is unhelpful. The main one I want to explore here is that, somehow, oracy is pitted against knowledge.

Oracy to me is predominantly about learning through talk, largely exploratory talk – and, because there are many structures and aspects to talk that help everyone to engage, learning to talk is also embedded in that

We don’t get knowledge and then speak; there’s no neat linear sequence. As we talk about ideas, we engage with them, we connect new and existing knowledge, stretch our schema around and in so doing, we strengthen our understanding.

I see it all the time – students barely given time to grapple with ideas that are half formed, barely given a chance to explore their own understanding and not guided down a path where, by listening to others and exchanging ideas about the topic in hand, they would be able to strengthen their understanding.
Inclusion means that everyone is learning. That means that, with talk, everyone needs to be talking.

You teach the pair-talk routines and expectations as you harness that talk structure to talk about hazards or sustainability or Othello. You teach how to probe deeply into the material intertwined with the material itself – just as you do when teaching how to write about different content.
You don’t just do talk for talk’s sake. You design appropriate talk activities that are most likely to elevate learning in the context of what you’re teaching.
It’s not extra, tick-boxed or an opportunity cost. It’s just a core feature of the whole learning process.

The concept of Consilience argues that reality itself has never been divided. Only our study of it has.

Science is not merely a way of asking questions; it is humanity’s collective memory of the answers we have discovered so far. Schools have the responsibility of ensuring every child inherits that memory before asking them to extend it.
Philosophies often begin with ideals about how learning ought to occur. Science begins by asking what actually happens when human beings learn.

A child is simultaneously a biological organism, a chemical system, a physical body and a social being. Therefore, to understand our students, we need to understand something about all of those things.

q: This is the central weakness in much American reform. We often demand better results from teachers without ensuring that preparation programs, state agencies, districts, licensure systems, and instructional program providers have given them the knowledge and tools needed to succeed.

Together, these groups can demand transparency, independent evidence audits, and accountability across the entire education system—not merely at the classroom level.

t: Cybersecurity Is Every Leader's Job
q: Too many organizations still treat cybersecurity as something only the IT department handles. That framing is convenient but dead wrong.

People trust leaders with their livelihoods, their personal information, and their reputations. Protecting that trust cannot be handed off entirely to specialists, any more than integrity can be relegated to the legal department.
Team members pay closer attention to what leaders do than to what policy says.
The team member who clicks a bad link and says so within minutes is an asset, not a problem child. The one who hides it for fear of blame can turn an incident into a serious breach.
Security is, and always has been, a set of choices about risk, and those choices belong at the leadership table, not solely with IT.
They require two approvals for large payments, confirm any change in account details through a second channel, and ensure access ends when a role ends.

t: 1983, Structured Literacy, and Systematic Phonics Instruction
q: So, I followed the directions in the teacher’s manual as if they were holy writ. In fact, I followed the directions with what we call “fidelity”. And because of my fidelity to the manual, I thought I was a good reading teacher.

What bothers me to this day is that I could have done so much better. I can still see the faces of the frustrated students who struggled to sound out words when they read and who couldn’t seem to put all letters in the correct order when they spelled words.
Educational jar-buzz are words and terms used in education and academia to create a façade of scholarly importance, intellectual authority, or theoretical sophistication (see Figure 1).
But all this really means is that there’s a scope and sequence. This is a list of teeny-tiny reading subskills (scope) laid out in the order in which they are to be taught (sequence).

Systematic phonics instruction is not more effective than unsystematic phonics instruction (Bowers, 2020; Camilli et al., 2006;). It is; however, significantly more boring than reading good books and learning phonics in this context.

While this may be appropriate for experimental research where control and treatment groups need to follow strict parameters in order to isolate a variable; it is neither effective nor appropriate when educating students in the uncontrolled confines of the real world.
And since real human beings are not standardized products, it would be educational malpractice to insist that teachers follow a recipe with “fidelity”.
